tool.name: AspectTransformation
tool.summary: Generates one or more transformations of an aspect raster at once: directional reclassifications (each cell assigned a named direction class in a Class attribute table) and trigonometric transforms (northness, eastness, and deviation from a chosen bearing). Built for aspect, supports D-infinity flow-direction rasters, and requires no Spatial Analyst.
tool.usage:
Aspect -- the compass direction a slope faces -- is often more useful after transformation, either grouped into a few named classes or converted to a continuous number suitable for statistical analysis (aspect itself is circular, so it cannot be used directly as a linear predictor). This tool offers both, and can produce several transformations in a single run; each becomes its own output raster in the chosen output location, named from a base name plus a suffix.
Reclassifications (integer rasters with a Class attribute table). Each cell is assigned to a named direction class, written to the output's value attribute table in a "Class" text field: • North / South: North for cells with a northward component (cosine of aspect >= 0), South otherwise. Cells facing exactly east or west are assigned to North. • East / West: East for cells with an eastward component (sine of aspect >= 0), West otherwise. Cells facing exactly north or south are assigned to East. • North / East / South / West: 90-degree classes centered on the cardinal directions (North = 315-45, East = 45-135, South = 135-225, West = 225-315). • Eight directions: 45-degree classes centered on the eight cardinal and intercardinal directions (North, Northeast, East, Southeast, South, Southwest, West, Northwest).
Flat cells (aspect -1) form their own "Flat" class (value -1) unless the flat option is set to NoData. The reclass outputs are symbolized with a direction color scheme.
Trigonometric transforms (continuous, double-precision rasters): • Northness: the cosine of the aspect; 1 = due north, 0 = due east or west, -1 = due south. • Eastness: the sine of the aspect; 1 = due east, 0 = due north or south, -1 = due west. Northness and eastness together decompose aspect into its north-south and east-west components. • Trigonometric deviation from a bearing: the cosine of the difference between the aspect and a target bearing; 1 = facing exactly the target bearing, 0 = 90 degrees away, -1 = facing 180 degrees away. • Numeric deviation from a bearing: simply the angular difference in degrees between the aspect and the target bearing, from 0 (facing exactly the bearing) to 180 (facing directly away). See Jenness (2015).
The trigonometric deviation follows the aspect-transformation approach introduced for site-productivity research by Trimble and Weitzman (1956) -- whose original transform assigned the maximum value to the northeast (45 degrees) -- and generalized to any optimum bearing by Beers et al. (1966); the target bearing defaults to 45 degrees but can be set to whatever direction is most meaningful for your study.
Flat cells. Flat cells (aspect -1) have no direction. For the trigonometric transforms they are always written as NoData: -1 would be indistinguishable from a real value (due south for northness, due west for eastness, "facing away" for the deviation). For the reclassifications, the "Flat cells" option controls whether flat cells get their own Flat class (value -1) or are dropped to NoData.
Output and coordinate systems. Choose an output location (a folder or a geodatabase); each selected transformation is written there as a separate raster (base name + suffix, e.g. _NS, _8Dir, _Northness, _TrigDev135). Outputs are added to the map. The raster is processed in its own coordinate system (never projected).
D-infinity flow direction. A D-infinity (DINF) flow-direction raster is essentially an aspect raster -- the direction of steepest descent -- but in the mathematical convention (0 = east, counter-clockwise), not compass. Set "Input aspect convention" to Mathematical for such a raster and the aspect is converted to compass before every transformation. The tool suggests this automatically when it detects a DINF raster, and warns if the raster's values fall outside the aspect range (-1 to 360 degrees), which usually means the input is not aspect. (A standard D8 flow-direction raster stores flow codes 1-128, not degrees, and is not valid input.)
This tool honors no geoprocessing environments. References: Trimble and Weitzman (1956); Beers, Dress, and Wensel (1966); Jenness (2015); and, for the sine/cosine decomposition and circular data generally, Jenness (2012).

dialogReference.para: A single-band aspect raster in degrees, 0-360 measured clockwise from north (compass), with -1 for flat cells. A D-infinity flow-direction raster is also valid -- set the Input aspect convention to Mathematical for it.

One or more transformations to generate (each produces its own output raster). Reclassifications (North/South, East/West, four directions, eight directions) create integer rasters with a Class attribute table; the trigonometric transforms (northness, eastness, deviation from a bearing) create continuous double-precision rasters. See the tool description for each.
The folder or geodatabase where the output rasters are written. Defaults to the input raster's workspace.

The base name for the outputs; each transformation adds a suffix (e.g. _NS, _8Dir, _Northness, _TrigDev135). Defaults to the input raster's name. Names are made valid for the output workspace and uniquified.

param.name: target_bearing
param.displayname: Target bearing (deg, for the deviation transforms)

dialogReference.para: The reference bearing (0-360 degrees) for the two deviation transforms: the direction that scores 1 (trigonometric deviation) or 0 (numeric deviation). Defaults to 45 degrees (northeast, the optimum in Trimble and Weitzman's original oak study). Used only when a deviation transform is selected.

The angular convention of the input. Choose Compass for an ordinary aspect raster (0 = north, clockwise). Choose Mathematical for a D-infinity flow-direction raster (0 = east, counter-clockwise); the aspect is converted to compass before transformation. The tool suggests Mathematical automatically when it detects a D-infinity raster.

How to treat flat cells (aspect -1, no direction) in the reclassifications: keep them as their own Flat class (value -1), or drop them to NoData. The trigonometric transforms always write flat cells as NoData regardless of this setting, because -1 is a valid data value there.

scriptExample.title: Aspect Transformation example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Generate several transformations at once. transformations is a list; valid values are exactly: "Reclassify: North / South", "Reclassify: East / West", "Reclassify: North / East / South / West", "Reclassify: 8 directions (N / NE / E / SE / S / SW / W / NW)", "Northness (cosine of aspect; 1 = north, -1 = south)", "Eastness (sine of aspect; 1 = east, -1 = west)", "Trigonometric deviation from a bearing (1 = toward, -1 = away)", "Numeric deviation from a bearing (degrees, 0 - 180)". input_convention: "Compass (0 = north, clockwise)", "Mathematical (0 = east, counter-clockwise; e.g. D-infinity)". flat_handling: "Reclassifications keep a Flat class (trig transforms are NoData at flat cells)", "All transforms: flat cells -> NoData".
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
arcpy.jenness.AspectTransformation( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\aspect", transformations=["Reclassify: 8 directions (N / NE / E / SE / S / SW / W / NW)", "Northness (cosine of aspect; 1 = north, -1 = south)", "Trigonometric deviation from a bearing (1 = toward, -1 = away)"], out_workspace=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb", base_name="aspect", target_bearing=45, input_convention="Compass (0 = north, clockwise)", flat_handling="All transforms: flat cells -> NoData")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Generates directional reclassifications (with a Class attribute table) and trigonometric transforms (northness, eastness, deviation from a bearing) of an aspect raster; multiple at once; D-infinity supported; no Spatial Analyst.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Transforms an aspect raster in one or more ways at once. Reclassifications assign each cell a named direction class (North/South, East/West, four directions, or eight directions) written to a Class value-attribute-table field; flat cells (-1) form a Flat class or become NoData. Trigonometric transforms create continuous double-precision rasters: northness (cosine; 1 = north, -1 = south), eastness (sine; 1 = east, -1 = west), trigonometric deviation from a target bearing (cosine of the difference; 1 = toward, -1 = away; Trimble and Weitzman 1956, Beers et al. 1966), and numeric deviation in degrees (0-180; Jenness 2015). The target bearing defaults to 45 degrees (northeast). D-infinity flow-direction rasters -- essentially aspect in the mathematical convention -- are supported via a convention toggle. No Spatial Analyst is required. See also Jenness (2012) for the sine/cosine decomposition and circular data.
dataIdInfo.idCredit: Tool by Jeff Jenness, Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com). Methods: Trimble, G. R., Jr., and S. Weitzman. 1956. Site index studies of upland oaks in the northern Appalachians. Forest Science 2:162-173. Beers, T. W., P. E. Dress, and L. C. Wensel. 1966. Aspect transformation in site productivity research. Journal of Forestry 64(10):691-692. Jenness, J. 2015. Polar Plots for ArcGIS. Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com/arcgis/polar_plots.htm). See also Jenness, J. 2012, "Directions: making sense of directional data" (Jenness Enterprises). Suggested citation: Jenness, J. (2026). Aspect Transformation. Jenness Enterprises Wildlife Tools for ArcGIS Pro. Available at: http://www.jennessent.com.
